topics.title: Types of Requirements
topics.keyConcept: Requirements state what a system must do (functional) and how well or under what boundaries it must do it (non-functional). They are categorized by audience and domain details.
topics.content:
Requirements engineering is the process of establishing the services that the customer requires from a system and the constraints under which it operates. Requirements are classified as:

  • Functional Requirements: Statements of specific services the system must provide, detailing how it should react to particular inputs and behave in specific scenarios. Example: 'The system must send a password reset link to the registered email within 60 seconds of a request.'

  • Non-functional Requirements (NFRs): Constraints on the services or functions offered by the system, specifying quality attributes. They include speed, reliability, security, portability, and standards compliance. Example: 'The system database must encrypt all personally identifiable information (PII) using AES-256.'

  • Domain Requirements: Constraints and characteristics derived from the application domain rather than specific user requests. Example: In tax software, domain requirements dictate that tax calculations must comply with national tax laws.

  • User Requirements: Conceptual statements in natural language plus diagrams describing the system services and constraints, written primarily for business owners and clients.

  • System Requirements: Detailed specifications of the software's functional and non-functional behaviors, acting as the foundation for the technical design and contract between clients and developers.

Real-World Project Example: For an e-commerce platform, a functional requirement is 'users must be able to add items to a shopping cart'. A corresponding non-functional requirement is 'the shopping cart checkout transaction must process in less than 1.5 seconds under a load of 10,000 concurrent users'.
topics.commonMistakes: Treating Non-functional Requirements (NFRs) as optional. If an NFR like security or system performance is ignored, the system will fail to be adopted by users, even if all functional requirements work perfectly.
topics.interviewTip: Non-functional requirements (NFRs) are critical. If they are not met, the entire system can be useless, even if all functional requirements are correct. In system design interviews, always ask about scale, latency, availability, and security (NFRs) early.

topics.title: Requirement Elicitation & Analysis Techniques
topics.keyConcept: Elicitation is the process of gathering requirements from stakeholders through structured techniques like Interviews, Joint Application Design (JAD), Prototyping, and Observation.
topics.content:
Requirements elicitation is the process of collaborating with customers, users, and stakeholders to discover system requirements. Because users often struggle to express what they need, engineers use several techniques:

  • Interviews: Structured (closed) or unstructured (open) meetings. Unstructured interviews explore issues organically, while structured interviews follow a predefined set of questions.
  • Joint Application Design (JAD): A highly structured, facilitated workshop bringing together users, managers, and developers in a single room to collaboratively design and define requirements, significantly reducing elicitation time.
  • Prototyping: Building rapid mockups (wireframes, interactive click-throughs) of the user interface. This gives stakeholders a tangible model to critique, helping them uncover hidden requirements.
  • Ethnography / Observation: A technique where the software engineer spends time observing how users actually perform their daily work. This reveals implicit requirements and workflow workarounds that users might forget to mention during interviews.

Real-World Project Example: When designing a new inventory tracking system for a large warehouse, engineers utilize JAD sessions with warehouse managers to list core features, use prototypes to test the UI with forklift operators, and perform ethnography by shadow-observing operators in the warehouse to see how they handle damaged barcodes.
topics.commonMistakes: Relying solely on interviews. Users often describe their 'ideal' workflow rather than what actually happens. Observing users at work (ethnography) and showing them mockups (prototypes) are critical to finding the actual requirements.

topics.title: DFD, ERD, & Data Dictionaries
topics.keyConcept: System modeling uses DFDs to represent process flows, ERDs to model database entities, and Data Dictionaries to catalog all system metadata.
topics.content:
During requirements analysis, conceptual system models are constructed to organize information and communicate with stakeholders:

  • Data Flow Diagrams (DFDs): Visualize how data flows through processes, stores, and external entities. DFDs are structured hierarchically (Context Diagram -> Level 0 DFD -> Level 1 DFD). A Logical DFD focuses on business conceptual flow (what data moves, what transformations occur). A Physical DFD focuses on technical implementation details (which specific server scripts, folders, and database tables handle the data).
  • Entity-Relationship Diagrams (ERDs): Represent the system's logical database schema, defining entities (e.g., User, Order), their attributes (e.g., User ID, Email), and relationships (e.g., One User has Many Orders).
  • Data Dictionary: A centralized glossary containing metadata about all data items in the system. It catalogs data item names, data types (e.g., VARCHAR, INT), range of valid values, default values, and relationships.

Real-World Project Example: In an online streaming portal, a DFD shows the flow of video metadata from content publishers to user screens; the ERD maps how User Profiles relate to Subscriptions; and the Data Dictionary specifies that the field `subscription_status` must be a VARCHAR containing either 'active', 'suspended', or 'expired'.
topics.commonMistakes: Creating data flow diagrams where data moves directly between two external entities or two data stores without passing through a process. In DFD guidelines, data stores and external entities can only interact with processes.

topics.title: IEEE 830 SRS Document Walkthrough
topics.keyConcept: The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) is the official contract between clients and developers. The IEEE 830 standard defines its formal template and structure.
topics.content:
The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) is the baseline document that specifies everything the system must do. It is structured according to the **IEEE 830-1998** standard template, which is organized as follows:

  1. Introduction: Contains the document's Purpose, Scope of the software product, Definitions, Acronyms, and References.
  2. Overall Description: Explains the general factors that affect the product. It includes Product Perspective (interfaces to other hardware/software), Product Functions (high-level summary), User Characteristics, General Constraints, and Assumptions.
  3. Specific Requirements: Detailed technical specifications used by designers and developers. It includes:
    • External Interface Requirements (User, Hardware, Software, and Communication interfaces).
    • Functional Requirements (organized by mode, user class, or feature).
    • Performance Requirements (timing, throughput).
    • Design Constraints (compliance, hardware limits).
    • Software System Quality Attributes (Reliability, Availability, Security, Maintainability).

Feasibility Study: A preliminary assessment conducted before writing the SRS to determine if the project is operationally, technically, and economically viable. It determines if the system contributes to business goals and if it can be delivered within budget and technical limits.
topics.commonMistakes: Writing design decisions or code snippets in the SRS. The SRS must specify 'WHAT' the system must do, never 'HOW' it will be programmed or structured internally.
topics.interviewTip: If asked how to resolve conflicts between developer interpretations of requirements, refer to the SRS as the ultimate source of truth and contract baseline.

topics.title: Requirement Validation & Management
topics.keyConcept: Validation ensures the SRS reflects actual user needs, using formal reviews, prototypes, and automated test-case checks to find inconsistencies.
topics.content:
Requirement validation is concerned with showing that the requirements define the system that the customer really wants. Validation prevents requirements errors from cascading into costly design and coding fixes later in the SDLC. Techniques include:

  • Requirements Reviews (Inspections): A formal, systematic review where a team of developers, clients, and QA engineers check the SRS for clarity, completeness, consistency, and feasibility.
  • Prototyping: Demonstrating user-interface mockups to clients to verify that the specified workflows match their expectations.
  • Test-Case Generation: Designing system test cases directly from the SRS requirements. If a requirement is too vague to write a test case for, it indicates that the requirement must be rewritten for clarity.

Requirement Management: The process of managing changing requirements during system development. It uses traceability matrices to link requirements to design modules, source code files, and test cases, ensuring that any requirement change automatically propagates to the correct code sections.
topics.commonMistakes: Performing validation only at the end of the project. Requirements validation must occur during the requirements gathering phase (specifically reviewing drafts of the SRS) to catch defects early when they are cheap to correct.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the difference between Functional and Non-functional requirements? Give examples.
practiceQuestions.answer: Functional requirements define specific behaviors or services the system must perform (e.g., 'The system must send an email notification when a payment is processed'). Non-functional requirements specify quality attributes or constraints (e.g., 'The system database must be encrypted' or 'The page load time must be under 1.5 seconds').

practiceQuestions.question: Describe the difference between Logical DFD and Physical DFD.
practiceQuestions.answer: A Logical DFD describes the system's data flows and transformations from a business/conceptual perspective, independent of hardware or software implementation. A Physical DFD shows the actual implementation details, specifying folders, servers, physical databases, and specific programs that execute data transfers.

practiceQuestions.question: What is a Data Dictionary and why is it important during requirements engineering?
practiceQuestions.answer: A Data Dictionary is a centralized repository of metadata that defines the names, descriptions, structures, types, and validation rules of all data elements in a system. It is important because it prevents naming conflicts, ensures consistency across teams, and serves as a reference for database designers and developers.

practiceQuestions.question: Explain the purpose of a Feasibility Study in software development.
practiceQuestions.answer: A Feasibility Study evaluates if the project is viable before committing significant budget and resources. It examines technical feasibility (can we build it?), operational feasibility (will it solve the business problem?), and economic feasibility (is the return on investment positive?).

practiceQuestions.question: What is an SRS document and which standard defines its structure?
practiceQuestions.answer: A Software Requirements Specification (SRS) is a formal document describing the system's complete functional and non-functional requirements. Its structure is standardized by the IEEE 830 standard, which includes sections for Introduction, General Description, and Specific Requirements.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a functional requirement?
options: The system must load pages in under 2 seconds
The system must allow users to register with a valid email address
The system database must be hosted on AWS
The system must comply with GDPR guidelines
mcqs.explanation: Registering an account is a functional capability/service provided by the system to the user. The others are constraints (non-functional requirements).

mcqs.question: Constraints on response time, reliability, and security are categorized as what type of requirements?
mcqs.explanation: Non-functional requirements specify quality constraints, system attributes, and boundaries under which the system must operate.

mcqs.question: Which system diagram models the processing steps and the movement of data between processes and external entities?
mcqs.explanation: DFDs visualize the flow of data through processes, data stores, and external entities.

mcqs.question: What is the primary document used to establish a contract between the client and developers regarding system requirements?
mcqs.explanation: The SRS serves as the official agreement defining the exact scope of software development and requirements.

mcqs.question: Which IEEE standard guidelines are commonly used for structuring the SRS?
mcqs.explanation: IEEE 830 is the widely adopted standard for organizing and writing Software Requirements Specifications.

mcqs.question: A feasibility study is conducted during which phase of software development?
options: Right before writing the user manual
mcqs.explanation: A feasibility study is a preliminary investigation conducted at the very beginning to decide if the project is viable and should proceed.

mcqs.question: A Logical DFD does which of the following?
options: Shows physical folders and database tables
Focuses on business functions and flow of data conceptually
Shows exact server hardware IP addresses
mcqs.explanation: Logical DFDs represent business processes conceptually and ignore technical implementation details.

mcqs.question: A centralized store containing names, types, constraints, and descriptions of all data structures is called what?
mcqs.explanation: A Data Dictionary is a centralized glossary of all data items, their formats, structures, and business definitions.

mcqs.question: Which requirements engineering activity involves checking if the requirements define the system the customer truly wants?
mcqs.explanation: Validation ensures the requirements actually represent user needs and are free from inconsistencies, ambiguities, and omissions.

mcqs.question: Domain requirements are unique because they:
options: Are derived from the application domain's physics or regulations rather than specific user requests
Are always written in assembly language
mcqs.explanation: Domain requirements reflect constraints of the application domain itself (e.g., standard banking interest rules, aircraft flight physics regulations).
